stories.title: Durian trade is a high-stakes hustle in Chinese border town
stories.summary: PINGXIANG, Guangxi – Su Wenpeng once drove a small lorry ferrying durians from Vietnam to China, but that hustle no longer works, he says. Chinese people are consuming so much of the fruit that each shipment now needs a freight truck many times the size. These days, “everything is shipped by the container”, said Su, who has since sold his lorry and drives trucks for a logistics company instead. The old way of “using small vehicles like ants moving houses – that doesn’t exist any more”. China relies heavily on South-east Asia to feed its durian habit, producing less than 1 per cent of the fruit it imported in 2025. It imported a million tonnes of durian in the first half of 2026, up 51.6 per cent year on year, mostly from Thailand and Vietnam. A third of that was driven into China through the small town of Pingxiang, located on the border with Vietnam. It is a transit point that offers a window into how some in China are making a living from their compatriots’ taste for the “king of fruit”. On a recent weekday afternoon, trucks carrying tonnes of the spiky fruit trundled in through the checkpoint and stopped at transfer stations nearby. Dozens of workers lifted boxes out of the Vietnamese vehicles and into Chinese ones to be sent to stores and markets across the country. Traders bent over samples of the fruit, inspecting them with flashlights and knocking on their shells with a hammer-like contraption. Based on the thudding sounds, they can judge if the durians are ripe.
